This project examines the relationship between the U.S. stock market and the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield from 2000 through 2026. The S&P 500 is used to represent stock-market performance, while the 10-year Treasury yield represents conditions in the U.S. bond market. Historical S&P 500 data were obtained through Yahoo Finance, while Treasury yield data were collected from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED). Using R, I analyze the relationship between daily S&P 500 returns and changes in the 10-year Treasury yield, with particular attention to how this relationship changed during the 2008–2009 Financial Crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 market shock.

## Regression output


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(quantmod)
library(fredr)
library(tidyverse)

model1 <- lm(
  sp500_return ~ treasury10_change, 
  data = stock_bond_clean
)

summary(model1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
lm(formula = sp500_return ~ treasury10_change, data = stock_bond_clean)

Residuals:
      Min        1Q    Median        3Q       Max 
-0.107593 -0.005202  0.000261  0.005624  0.101562 

Coefficients:
                   Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       0.0003357  0.0001421   2.363   0.0182 *  
treasury10_change 0.0599212  0.0024619  24.339   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.01155 on 6598 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.08239,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.08225 
F-statistic: 592.4 on 1 and 6598 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
```


:::
:::


:::

::: {.finding}
A linear regression of daily S&P 500 returns on daily changes in the 10-year Treasury yield from 2000–2026 found a statistically significant positive association (β = 0.060, p \< 0.001). However, the model's R² of 0.082 indicates that Treasury yield changes alone explain only a small portion of daily equity-return variation.
:::

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:

Residuals:
      Min        1Q    Median        3Q       Max 
-0.108047 -0.006451  0.001057  0.006853  0.079937 

Coefficients:

```


:::
:::


:::



::: {.finding}
The relationship between S&P 500 returns and changes in 10-year Treasury yields strengthened during periods of major financial stress. This is reflected in the increase in R² from 0.082 during 2000–2026 to 0.1495 during the 2008–2009 Financial Crisis and 0.2303 during the 2020 COVID-19 period. Thus, changes in Treasury yields explained a greater proportion of the variation in daily S&P 500 returns during both crises.
:::

## What changed after 2022?

The crisis models treat each period as a separate window. To see how the relationship moved over time, I calculated the correlation between daily S&P 500 returns and daily changes in the 10-year Treasury yield over a rolling window of the previous 250 trading days, about one year.




::: {.cell .column-page}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/Rolling_graph-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of the rolling one-year correlation between daily S&P 500 returns and daily 10-year Treasury yield changes, 2001 to 2026. It stays mostly between 0.2 and 0.6, with shaded bands for the 2008 to 2009 crisis and 2020, then drops below zero for most of the period after 2022.' width=2200}
:::
:::


::: {.finding}
From 2001 through 2021, the rolling correlation averaged 0.34 and was positive on 94% of trading days: stocks tended to rise on days when Treasury yields rose. Since 2022, a period that began as the Federal Reserve started raising interest rates, that pattern has broken down. The correlation averaged -0.05, was negative on 62% of trading days, and reached -0.31 in July 2024. In the most recent period, rising yields have more often coincided with falling stock prices, the opposite of the pattern that held for the previous two decades. Like the regressions above, this measures association, not cause.
:::
